title: Densest admissible patterns of primes n^2 + h
statement: Call a set H of positive integers admissible for n^2 + h if for every prime p there is an integer n with n^2 + h not divisible by p for all h in H; equivalently, the residues -h (mod p) miss at least one of the (p+1)/2 values of n^2 (mod p), 0 included. Only primes p <= 2|H| - 1 need checking. Admissibility is necessary for n^2 + h to be prime for all h in H at once for infinitely many n, and by the Bateman-Horn conjecture it is sufficient. Let m(k) be the least m such that some admissible k-set lies in [1, m]. Determine m(k); the headline cell is k = 50: find an admissible 50-set with largest element below 247.
submission: Text file: 50 distinct positive integers h, separated by spaces or newlines (lines starting with # are ignored).
score: the largest element of the set (smaller is better)

best_known.source: Quantavane (Arhan Canli), 9 November 2026: an admissible 50-set with largest element 247 found by a randomized greedy sieve (tools/quad_sieve.py: for each prime p <= 99 delete the h whose -h falls in the least used square class)

context: For linear shifts n + h, the least width of an admissible k-tuple, H(k), is the classical quantity behind bounded gaps between primes (Engelsma's and Sutherland's tables; Polymath8b). Quadratic families are the next case of the Bateman-Horn conjecture: whether n^2 + 1 is prime infinitely often is one of Landau's problems, and Hardy and Littlewood's Conjecture F gives the predicted density. The dense patterns here are the quadratic analogue of prime k-tuples: {1, 3, 7, 9} gives 5, 7, 11, 13 at n = 2, and the question is how tightly k such polynomials can be packed without a fixed prime divisor. Admissibility for n^2 + h is a covering condition on the square classes modulo each prime (a class is blocked by every h with -h in it), so it differs from the linear case already at p = 3, where only the classes 0 and 1 need covering.
references: P. T. Bateman, R. A. Horn, A heuristic asymptotic formula concerning the distribution of prime numbers, Math. Comp. 16 (1962) 363-367
G. H. Hardy, J. E. Littlewood, Some problems of 'Partitio numerorum' III, Acta Math. 44 (1923) 1-70 (Conjecture F on n^2 + 1)
D. H. J. Polymath, Variants of the Selberg sieve, and bounded intervals containing many primes, arXiv:1407.4897 (H(k) for linear tuples)
W. Banks, K. Ford, Sets of integers satisfying Bateman-Horn statistics, arXiv:2605.01155
A. Kourbatov, M. Wolf, Predicting maximal gaps in sets of primes, arXiv:1901.03785 (densest linear patterns)

novelty.verdict: new. No table or study of least admissible shift sets for the family n^2 + h was found (arXiv, web search); the sequence m(k) is not in the OEIS. Densest admissible tuples are studied only for linear shifts.
closest: Linear admissible k-tuples and their least width H(k) (Engelsma, Sutherland, Polymath8b; Kourbatov and Wolf on densest patterns, arXiv:1901.03785): the linear case of this problem.

first_values.note: Exact values by exhaustive search (tools/quad_admissible.py, sets with largest element m for increasing m); the sieve (tools/quad_sieve.py) reproduces every exact value and gives the upper bounds for larger k.

baseline.text: 247 for k = 50, held by Quantavane (Arhan Canli), 9 November 2026: the set in `refs/quad-admissible.txt`. Lower bound: m(50) >= m(19) = 77 (removing elements keeps a set admissible); nothing better is proved.

bound.source: m(k) is non-decreasing and m(19) = 77 exactly
